17.01.title: Why CFD and what it can't do
17.01.html:
Computational fluid dynamics turns the Navier-Stokes equations into numbers on a grid. It shows what no wind tunnel can (pressure everywhere, flow inside a pump), and it is cheap to vary a design. It also produces beautiful, wrong pictures with great confidence. This phase builds solvers from scratch so you know where the errors come from.

Three kinds of error

Every CFD result differs from reality by a sum of contributions:

ϕcomputed​−ϕreal​=modelling(ϕmodel​−ϕreal​)​​+discretisation(ϕh​−ϕmodel​)​​+round-off and iteration(ϕcomputed​−ϕh​)​​.
  • Modelling error: the equations you solve are not the real ones. Turbulence models, a neglected heat source, an assumed inlet profile, rigid walls.
  • Discretisation error: the grid and time step are finite. It falls with refinement at the scheme’s order, ε≈Chp, so it can be estimated from two or three grids (Richardson extrapolation).
  • Round-off and iteration error: floating-point arithmetic and stopping an iterative solver early. Round-off grows as the grid gets finer, so refinement eventually stops helping.

Refining the grid only attacks the second term. No amount of mesh fixes a wrong model, which is why validation against experiments (17.17) is separate from verification of the numerics.

Stability is not accuracy

Some schemes produce nonsense outright. Central differences for advection-diffusion oscillate when the cell Peclet number Peh​=Uh/Γ exceeds 2. Explicit schemes blow up above a Courant limit (17.02). These failures are obvious; the dangerous errors are the smooth, plausible ones.

Worked exampleAn error budget that adds up

The real problem is uϕ′−Γϕ′′=s on [0,1] with ϕ(0)=0, ϕ(1)=1, u=1, Γ=0.05 (Pe = 20) and a small source s=0.05. The model leaves the source out and uses central differences. The quantity of interest is ϕ(0.9).

Each contribution is estimated without knowing the true answer: modelling by a sensitivity run with the source switched on, discretisation by Richardson extrapolation from N and 2N intervals, round-off by repeating the solve in float64.

Grid, precision Modelling Discretisation Round-off Budget Observed
20, float64 −0.038304 −0.024652 0 −0.062956 −0.062457
40, float64 −0.038251 −0.005760 0 −0.044010 −0.043969
40, float32 −0.038251 −0.005760 +1.9×10−8 −0.044010 −0.043968
2000, float32 −0.038233 −0.000002 −1.8×10−4 −0.038417 −0.038417
  1. The budget matches the observed error to within 1 % in every case.
  2. From 20 to 40 intervals, the discretisation error falls by 4.3 times (order 2), but the modelling error does not move.
  3. At 2000 intervals in float32, round-off has grown to 100 times the discretisation error.
  4. With 8 intervals the cell Peclet number is 2.5, and the solution dips to −0.111: an unphysical wiggle.

Exercise 1When to stop refining

A second-order scheme has a discretisation error of 4×10−3 at N=50. The modelling error is about 2×10−2. How many intervals bring the discretisation error below one tenth of the modelling error?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Target: 2×10−3, half the current value.
  2. Error ∝N−2, so N=502​=70.7; use N=71.
  3. Refining further buys almost nothing: the answer is dominated by the model.

17.02.title: Conservation form and finite volumes
17.02.html:
Mass, momentum and energy are conserved: what leaves one region enters the next. The finite-volume method builds this into the discretisation, which is why nearly every industrial CFD code (OpenFOAM, Fluent, STAR-CCM+) uses it.

Integral form and cell averages

A conservation law ∂t​q+∂x​f(q)=0, integrated over a cell [xi−1/2​,xi+1/2​], becomes exact bookkeeping:

dtd​∫xi−1/2​xi+1/2​​qdx=f(xi−1/2​)−f(xi+1/2​).

Store the cell average Qi​. With a numerical flux Fi+1/2​ at each face and forward Euler in time:

Qin+1​=Qin​−ΔxΔt​(Fi+1/2​−Fi−1/2​).

Summed over all cells, the face fluxes cancel in pairs (telescoping), so on a periodic domain ∑i​Qi​Δx never changes, apart from round-off. That holds for any flux formula; accuracy and stability depend on the choice.

The upwind flux

For advection f=aq with a>0, information comes from the left, so take Fi+1/2​=aQi​. The scheme is stable for Courant number c=aΔt/Δx≤1: the fluid must not travel more than one cell per step (the CFL condition).

Conservative against advective form. With a variable speed a(x), the conservation law is qt​+(aq)x​=0. The advective equation qt​+aqx​=0 is a different equation: it transports values along the flow but does not conserve the total. Discretising the wrong form is a classic bug.

Worked exampleDye in a periodic channel

200 cells on [0,1], a=1, a Gaussian bump plus a block of dye, Courant number 0.8.

  1. Once around the domain (250 steps): the total ∑Qi​Δx=0.325331413609785 drifts by at most 5.6×10−17.
  2. The values stay between 0 and 1: upwind with c≤1 makes each new value a weighted average of old ones, Qin+1​=(1−c)Qi​+cQi−1​.
  3. At c=1.2 the weights are no longer positive, and after half a period the solution has grown to 1.5×1011.
  4. Variable speed a=1+0.5sin2πx, 400 steps: the conservative form keeps the total at 0.125331413610; the advective form drifts to 0.048193.

Exercise 1One step by hand

Cells hold Q=[0,1,1,0] (periodic), a=1, c=0.5. Do one upwind step and check the total.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Fluxes through the right faces: F/a=Q=[0,1,1,0].
  2. Qinew​=Qi​−0.5(Qi​−Qi−1​): [0−0.5(0−0),1−0.5(1−0),1−0.5(1−1),0−0.5(0−1)]=[0,0.5,1,0.5].
  3. Total: 2 before and 0+0.5+1+0.5=2 after.

Largest stable time step (ms) for upwind advection with a = 5 m/s and Δx = 2 cm.
New value of a cell holding 1 after one upwind step at c = 0.25, with its left neighbour holding 0. 2 decimals.

17.03.title: Flux schemes
17.03.html:
The finite-volume update is only as good as its face flux. First-order upwind is robust but smears everything; second-order schemes are sharper but wiggle near jumps. TVD limiters combine the two.

Upwind and Lax-Wendroff

For advection with speed a>0 and Courant number c=aΔt/Δx, write the face flux as upwind plus a correction:

Fi+1/2​=a[Qi​+21​(1−c)ϕ(ri​)(Qi+1​−Qi​)],ri​=Qi+1​−Qi​Qi​−Qi−1​​.
  • ϕ=0: upwind, first order, adds numerical diffusion 21​aΔx(1−c).
  • ϕ=1: Lax-Wendroff, second order, but dispersive: it creates over- and undershoots at jumps.

Godunov’s theorem says no linear scheme can be both better than first order and free of new extrema. The way out is a nonlinear ϕ(r) that depends on the local smoothness ratio r.

TVD limiters

The total variation TV=∑i​∣Qi+1​−Qi​∣ measures how wiggly the solution is. A scheme is TVD (total variation diminishing) if TV never grows; then no new extrema can appear. Harten and Sweby showed that the scheme above is TVD when 0≤ϕ(r)≤min(2r,2), and second order in smooth regions when ϕ(1)=1.

Limiter ϕ(r)
minmod max(0,min(1,r))
van Leer (r+∣r∣)/(1+∣r∣)
superbee max(0,min(2r,1),min(r,2))

Minmod is the most diffusive of the three, superbee the most compressive (it sharpens fronts, and can square off smooth peaks).

Worked exampleA square pulse once around

200 cells, c=0.5, a pulse of height 1 on 0.2<x<0.5, 400 steps.

Scheme Min Max Total variation (starts at 2) Mean error
upwind 0.00000 0.99731 1.9946 0.0797
Lax-Wendroff −0.23210 1.23206 3.9352 0.0523
minmod 0.00000 1.00000 2.0000 0.0314
van Leer 0.00000 1.00000 2.0000 0.0204
superbee 0.00000 1.00000 2.0000 0.0088
  1. The four TVD schemes never leave [0,1], and their total variation never grows at any step.
  2. Lax-Wendroff overshoots by 23 % and almost doubles the total variation.
  3. Superbee is nine times more accurate than upwind on this discontinuous profile.

Exercise 1Evaluating limiters

At a cell where Qi−1​=0.2, Qi​=0.5, Qi+1​=0.6, find r and the minmod, van Leer and superbee values of ϕ.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. r=(0.5−0.2)/(0.6−0.5)=3.
  2. Minmod: max(0,min(1,3))=1.
  3. Van Leer: (3+3)/(1+3)=1.5.
  4. Superbee: max(0,min(6,1),min(3,2))=2.

Van Leer limiter value at r = 0.5. 4 decimals.
Total variation of the cell values [0, 1, 1, 0, 0] on a periodic domain.

17.04.title: "Burgers' equation and shocks"
17.04.html:
In linear advection every part of the profile moves at the same speed. In a real flow the speed depends on the solution itself, and fast parts overtake slow ones. Inviscid Burgers' equation is the simplest model of this:

ut​+(21​u2)x​=0,or, where smooth,ut​+uux​=0.

Characteristics and shock formation

Where the solution is smooth, u is constant along characteristics dx/dt=u, which are straight lines: u(x,t)=u0​(x−ut). Where u0​ decreases, faster fluid behind catches up, the profile steepens, and the characteristics cross at

t∗=max(−u0′​)1​.

After t∗ the smooth solution would be multivalued; instead a shock forms. Conservation across the jump fixes its speed (the Rankine-Hugoniot condition):

s=uL​−uR​f(uL​)−f(uR​)​=2uL​+uR​​.

Only a conservative scheme converges to shocks at the correct speed; this is the deepest reason for the finite-volume form.

The Rusanov flux

A robust numerical flux for any conservation law is Rusanov (local Lax-Friedrichs):

Fi+1/2​=21​[f(uL​)+f(uR​)]−21​a(uR​−uL​),a=max(∣uL​∣,∣uR​∣),

the average flux plus just enough dissipation for the fastest local wave. With a minmod-limited linear reconstruction of uL​, uR​ (MUSCL) and a two-stage Runge-Kutta step, it is second order in smooth regions and holds shocks to about two cells.

Worked exampleA shock forming and moving

  1. Riemann problem u=1 for x<0, 0 for x>0, 400 cells on [−1,3]: Rankine-Hugoniot gives s=0.5. The computed shock is at x=0.505 at t=1 and 1.005 at t=2 (cell size 0.01). The mass gained, 0.5 and 1.0, equals the inflow f(1)t=t/2.
  2. Sine u0​=1+0.5sin2πx, periodic, 800 cells. max(−u0′​)=π, so t∗=1/π=0.3183.
  3. Before t∗ the steepest slope is π/(1−t/t∗): at 0.5t∗, 6.30 against 6.28. After t∗ it jumps to about 290, limited only by the grid.
  4. At 2t∗, the states on either side of the shock are 1.469 and 0.530, so s=0.999; by symmetry the shock moves at 1, starting from x=0.5. Predicted position 0.1366 (wrapping around), computed 0.1362. The mean of u stays exactly 1.000000000000.

Exercise 1When does it break?

Traffic-like data: u0​=2 for x<0, falling linearly to 1 at x=0.5, then 1. When does a shock form, and how fast does it then move?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. The slope is u0′​=−1/0.5=−2, so t∗=1/2=0.5.
  2. At t∗ all characteristics from the ramp meet at once, and the shock separates uL​=2 from uR​=1.
  3. Its speed is (2+1)/2=1.5.

quiz.q: Shock formation time for u₀ = 1 + 0.2 sin(2πx). 4 decimals.
Rankine-Hugoniot speed of a Burgers shock between u_L = 3 and u_R = 1.
Rusanov flux for Burgers with u_L = 1, u_R = 0. 2 decimals.
Along a characteristic of inviscid Burgers' equation, u is:
quiz.explain: The characteristics are straight lines of speed u.

17.05.title: Shallow water and the dam break
17.05.html:
Rivers, floods, tides and irrigation channels are shallow: much wider than deep. Averaging the flow over the depth turns the 3D Navier-Stokes equations into the shallow water (Saint-Venant) system, a conservation law for depth h and discharge q=hu:

∂t∂​[hhu​]+∂x∂​[huhu2+21​gh2​]=[0−ghzb′​−friction​].

The assumption is a hydrostatic pressure, p=ρg(h−z): vertical accelerations are small. Waves travel at u±gh​, so this is a hyperbolic system like Burgers' equation, but with two families of waves.

The dam break

At t=0 a wall at x=0 holding water of depth h0​ vanishes. On a dry bed the exact answer is Ritter’s solution (1892), a single rarefaction fan:

h(x,t)=9g1​(2gh0​​−tx​)2,−gh0​​t≤x≤2gh0​​t.

The water at the dam site sits at 4h0​/9 for all time, the disturbance travels upstream at gh0​​, and the dry front runs downstream at 2gh0​​. If the bed downstream is wet with depth hR​, Stoker’s solution adds a bore (a moving hydraulic jump): a rarefaction, a flat plateau hm​, then a shock whose speed follows from Rankine-Hugoniot.

The scheme

Finite volumes with the HLL flux (Harten, Lax, van Leer): two wave-speed estimates sL​<sR​ bound the Riemann fan, and the flux is the conservative average in between. On a dry side, sR​=uL​+2ghL​​ (Toro) captures the dry front speed. Minmod reconstruction and RK2 give second order in smooth regions; depths are clipped at zero (a no-op at this CFL apart from round-off).

Worked exampleConverging to Ritter

h0​=1 m, g=9.81 m/s², t=0.5 s, so gh0​​=3.1321 m/s.

Cells L1 error in h Depth at the dam Mass
200 0.03578 0.4579 5.0000000000
400 0.01839 0.4515 5.0000000000
800 0.00930 0.4481 5.0000000000
1600 0.00468 0.4463 5.0000000000
  1. The observed order is 0.96, 0.98, 0.99: first order, as expected for a solution with kinks at the edges of the fan. “Second order” schemes only reach second order where the solution is smooth.
  2. The depth at the dam converges to 4/9=0.4444.
  3. The front is the hardest part: the exact 1 mm contour is at 2.9835 m, the computed one at 2.853 m with 1600 cells. Near a dry front the depth goes to zero and so does the wave speed, so every scheme lags a little.
  4. Stoker, hR​=0.1 m: the plateau is 0.3962 m at 2.3214 m/s and the bore moves at 3.1051 m/s. With 800 cells the computed plateau is 0.3962 m and the bore sits at 1.5563 m against 1.5526 m.

Exercise 1A real dam

A 20 m deep reservoir fails onto a dry valley. How fast does the front travel, and how deep is the water at the dam site?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. gh0​​=9.81×20​=14.0 m/s.
  2. The ideal front speed is 2gh0​​=28.0 m/s, about 100 km/h. Real fronts are slower because bed friction (neglected by Ritter) dominates in the thin tip.
  3. The depth at the dam is 4×20/9=8.9 m.

17.06.title: 2D shallow water on Subak terraces
17.06.html:
Bali’s Subak rice terraces move water from a shared canal down a staircase of flooded paddies, each held by a low earthen bund. Simulating that needs the 2D shallow water equations and three things the dam break did not:

  1. Bed slope. The source term −gh∇zb​ must balance the pressure gradient exactly in still water.
  2. Wet and dry cells. Most of the domain starts dry and fronts move across it.
  3. Exact conservation. Water is a shared, scarce resource; the model must not create or lose it.

Hydrostatic reconstruction

A naive discretisation of −gh∂zb​/∂x does not cancel the discrete flux of 21​gh2, so a lake at rest starts sloshing. Audusse et al. (2004) fix this at every face: with face bed level zf​=max(zL​,zR​), use reconstructed depths

hL∗​=max(0,hL​+zL​−zf​),hR∗​=max(0,hR​+zR​−zf​)

in the flux, and add 21​g(hL2​−hL∗2​) to the momentum flux on the left side (and similarly on the right). The scheme is then

  • well balanced: still water stays still to round-off, even with a shoreline;
  • positive: depths never go negative under the CFL condition, so wet/dry fronts need no special treatment;
  • conservative: the mass flux leaving one cell enters its neighbour.

Bed friction uses Manning’s law with n=0.03 s/m1/3, applied implicitly so it stays stable in very thin water. The walls of the domain reflect.

The terraces

Five terraces 8 m long and 12 m wide each step 0.4 m down, with a 6 cm bund at the downhill edge and a 0.5 % cross slope. A canal pours 20 L/s into the top corner. Explore the model interactively in the Subak lab.

Worked exampleFilling the staircase

0.5 m cells, 80 × 24.

  1. Lake at rest. Still water on every terrace, 1 cm below the lowest bund top, with dry strips on the high side of the cross slope (1520 of 1920 cells wet). After 60 s the largest discharge is 1.1×10−17 m²/s: round-off.
  2. Irrigation, from dry. The water in the domain always equals the inflow Qt: 1.2, 3.6, 6.0, 12.0 and 18.0 m³ at 60, 180, 300, 600 and 900 s, with the worst error over 4628 steps 1.9×10−13 m³. No depth ever goes negative.
  3. The cascade. Numbering the terraces 0 (top) to 4, the first litre reaches terraces 0 to 3 at 0, 171, 448 and 738 s; terrace 4 is still dry at 900 s. Each terrace must fill before it spills.
  4. A terrace holds about 5.9 m³ while it spills, twice its static capacity of 2.81 m³ up to the lowest bund top: the surface rides 3 to 5 cm above that point, the weir head needed to push 20 L/s over the bund.

Exercise 1Filling time

How long would one terrace of static capacity 2.81 m³ take to fill to the lowest bund top at 20 L/s, ignoring losses? Why does the simulation take longer for terrace 0 to spill?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. 2.81/0.02=140 s.
  2. Water first spreads over the dry terrace as a thin sheet and the surface must tilt to drive the flow, so the terrace stores more than the flat-pool volume before it spills; the first litre reached terrace 1 at 171 s.

Same face: the extra momentum flux ½g(h_L² − h_L*²) on the left side, in m³/s². 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: It is the pressure force of the water against the step.

quiz.q: Volume delivered by a 20 L/s inlet in 10 min, in m³.
quiz.explain: Q·t; the model holds exactly this.

17.07.title: "Incompressible flow: the lid-driven cavity"
17.07.html:
Incompressible Navier-Stokes has no equation for pressure: it is whatever keeps ∇⋅u=0. In 2D the cleanest way around this is to eliminate pressure altogether.

Streamfunction and vorticity

Define the streamfunction ψ with u=∂ψ/∂y, v=−∂ψ/∂x. Continuity then holds automatically. Taking the curl of the momentum equation removes the pressure and leaves a transport equation for the vorticity ω=∂v/∂x−∂u/∂y:

∂t∂ω​+u∂x∂ω​+v∂y∂ω​=Re1​∇2ω,∇2ψ=−ω.

Each time step:

  1. Set wall vorticity from the no-slip condition (Thom’s formula): ωw​=−2ψw+1​/h2, plus −2U/h on the moving lid.
  2. Advance ω in the interior (central differences, explicit Euler, Δt≤0.2h2Re and ≤0.5h/U).
  3. Solve the Poisson equation for ψ with ψ=0 on the walls.

Step 3 dominates the cost. On a uniform grid with Dirichlet walls the 5-point Laplacian is diagonalised by discrete sine transforms, λk​=(2cos(πk/N)−2)/h2, so a solve is two FFT-based transforms and a division: O(N2logN) and exact to round-off. The code checks it on a manufactured solution first.

The benchmark

A unit square with the lid sliding at U=1, Re=UL/ν=100. Ghia, Ghia and Shin (1982) give reference velocities on the centrelines and the primary vortex: ψmin​=−0.103423 at (0.6172,0.7344) on a 129 × 129 grid.

Worked exampleMatching Ghia at Re 100

Grid Steps to steady ψmin​ Vortex centre Max centreline deviation from Ghia
32 × 32 1800 −0.100381 (0.6230, 0.7431) 0.0309
64 × 64 5600 −0.102723 (0.6163, 0.7376) 0.0028
Ghia, 129 × 129 −0.103423 (0.6172, 0.7344)
  1. Doubling the grid cuts the gap in ψmin​ from 0.00304 to 0.00070, a factor 4.3: second order.
  2. On 64 × 64 the vortex centre is within a third of a cell of Ghia’s, and the centreline velocity within 0.003 everywhere (minimum −0.2115 against −0.2109).
  3. Steady state (“residual” max∣∂ω/∂t∣<10−6) takes about 27 time units: the lid must spin the fluid up against viscosity.

On a 64 × 64 grid at Re=100, which time-step limit is active? How many steps per unit time is that?

  2. Convection: 0.5h/U=0.5/64=0.00781.
  3. Diffusion is active: Δt=0.00488, about 205 steps per unit time, so the 27.3 time units took 5600 steps.

17.08.title: Projection methods on a staggered grid
17.08.html:
The streamfunction trick does not extend nicely to 3D. General incompressible solvers keep the primitive variables u,p and enforce continuity by projection (Chorin 1968).

Chorin’s method

The Helmholtz decomposition says any field splits into a divergence-free part and a gradient. Each step:

  1. Predict a velocity ignoring pressure: u∗=un+Δt[−(u⋅∇)u+Re1​∇2u]n.
  2. Solve the pressure Poisson equation ∇2p=∇⋅u∗/Δt, with ∂p/∂n=0 on walls.
  3. Project: un+1=u∗−Δt∇p. Then ∇⋅un+1=0.

Pressure is thus a Lagrange multiplier that removes the divergent part of u∗, defined only up to a constant.

Why a staggered grid

Store p at cell centres, u on vertical faces and v on horizontal faces (the MAC grid of Harlow and Welch). Then the discrete divergence, the gradient and the Poisson operator are consistent: discrete div of discrete grad equals the discrete Laplacian exactly, so step 3 makes the discrete divergence zero to round-off. On a collocated grid the same 5-point stencil decouples odd and even cells and lets a checkerboard pressure through.

The Neumann Laplacian on N cells is diagonalised by cosines, cos(πk(i+21​)/N) with eigenvalues −h24​sin22Nπk​. Its k=0 mode (a constant) has eigenvalue 0: that is the free constant in p, and it is dropped. The code diagonalises the matrix numerically once (64 × 64), so every Poisson solve is four matrix products.

Worked exampleThe cavity again, in primitive variables

Re 100, 64 × 64 MAC grid, same time-step rules as the streamfunction solver.

  1. Steady after 4600 steps (t=22.5).
  2. The largest ∣∇⋅u∣ after projection, over all steps, is 8.9×10−14; before projection, at the last step, it is 28.5. The curriculum’s target was below 10−8.
  3. Centreline u is within 0.0038 of Ghia (minimum −0.2128); ψmin​=−0.103179 at grid node (0.6094,0.7344), against −0.103423 at (0.6172,0.7344). Here ψ is integrated from u on the grid nodes, without sub-cell interpolation.
  4. The pressure range is 3.14, set by the singular top corners where the lid meets the walls.

Exercise 1A checkerboard

On a collocated 1D grid, the central gradient is (pi+1​−pi−1​)/2h. What does it give for pi​=(−1)i? What does the staggered gradient (pi+1​−pi​)/h give?

  2. Staggered: ((−1)i+1−(−1)i)/h=±2/h, the largest possible gradient, which the projection feels immediately.

17.09.title: Vortex shedding behind a cylinder
17.09.html:
Above Re≈47 the steady wake behind a cylinder becomes unstable and vortices peel off alternately from each side: the von Kármán vortex street. It makes telephone wires sing, chimneys sway and bridges oscillate. Its frequency is set by the Strouhal number

St=UfD​≈0.16 to 0.2for 60<Re<105.

Williamson’s fit for the laminar range is St=−3.3265/Re+0.1816+1.6×10−4Re, giving 0.164 at Re=100. When f approaches a structural natural frequency, the oscillation can lock in to it: the classic source of wind-induced vibration.

A solver that fits in a lesson

Body-fitted meshes around a cylinder take real meshing work. This lesson uses three shortcuts instead, all standard in research codes:

  1. Pseudo-spectral Navier-Stokes on a periodic box. Derivatives by FFT, the nonlinear term with 2/3 dealiasing and Adams-Bashforth 2, diffusion implicit (exact in Fourier space). The projection u^←u^−k(k⋅u^)/k2 makes ∇⋅u=0 to round-off.
  2. Brinkman penalisation. The cylinder is a region where a huge drag −λχu (λ=104, χ a smoothed mask) forces u→0. It is applied implicitly, so it is stable for any λ, and the force on the body is the momentum it removes.
  3. A fringe region. Near the outlet a sponge relaxes the flow back to (U,0), so the periodic box behaves like an inflow-outflow channel.

The box is 12D×6D, periodic in y: effectively a row of cylinders 6D apart (blockage 1/6). A small initial kick breaks the symmetry; the run lasts 100 D/U.

Worked exampleShedding at Re 100

Grid Steps Strouhal (lift) Wake probe spectrum Mean CD​ Lift amplitude
h=D/10, 120 × 60 5000 0.1585 0.160 2.84 0.89
h=D/16, 192 × 96 8000 0.1724 0.180 2.27 0.68
  1. The lift grows from an amplitude of 0.11 to 0.13 at 10<t<20 to its saturated value by t≈50; the Strouhal number is taken from the upward zero crossings of the lift for t>50 (period 5.80 D/U on the finer grid).
  2. Both grids give St inside the 0.16 to 0.2 band (the coarse grid only just), and the finer one is close to the 0.17 to 0.18 expected with 1/6 blockage, which raises the frequency above the unconfined 0.164.
  3. The wake-probe spectrum only resolves steps of 0.02 in St over 50 time units, so it is a cross-check, not a measurement.
  4. The drag is not trustworthy. Published CD​ at Re=100 is about 1.35 unconfined, and roughly 1.5 to 1.7 with this blockage; the solver gives 2.27 and falls with refinement. The smoothed mask makes a fatter, rougher body, and with 16 points per diameter the boundary layer is barely resolved. Frequency is a robust, global quantity; forces need a proper body-fitted mesh.
  5. max∣∇⋅u∣=1.3×10−16 throughout; the velocity inside the body stays below 0.027.

Exercise 1A singing wire

A 2 mm wire in a 10 m/s wind (ν=1.5×10−5 m²/s). Find Re and the shedding frequency, taking St=0.2.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Re=UD/ν=10×0.002/1.5×10−5=1333: well into the range where St≈0.2.
  2. f=StU/D=0.2×10/0.002=1000 Hz, an audible hum.

17.10.title: A coconut in an eddy
17.10.html:
A coconut drifting down a river reaches a boulder and gets stuck circling in the eddy behind it, sometimes for hours. Whether it escapes is a question about particle paths in the wake, which differ from streamlines whenever the flow is unsteady. Explore the scene in the Coconut lab.

Tracking passive particles

A small floating object that follows the surface flow obeys

dtdx​=u(x,t).

Integrate with Runge-Kutta, interpolating u from the grid bilinearly. (A real coconut also feels wind and inertia; here it is a perfect tracer.)

  • In a steady 2D flow, particles move along streamlines. A recirculation bubble has closed streamlines, so anything inside is trapped forever.
  • In an unsteady flow the closed streamlines break up. Fluid is exchanged across the bubble edge in “lobes” once per cycle, and particle paths become chaotic: chaotic advection.

So whether the coconut is trapped depends on whether the wake sheds.

A model of the steady bubble

Föppl (1913) found that a pair of opposite point vortices can sit stationary behind a cylinder of radius a in potential flow, anywhere on the curve

r−ra2​=2y,r=∣x∣,

with a definite strength Γ. With image vortices at a2/zˉ it satisfies no penetration on the cylinder exactly. The widget uses it as a kinematic model of the bubble and makes it unsteady by wobbling the two strengths in antiphase, Γ(1±εsinωt), like shedding.

Worked exampleTrapped or flushed

The penalised Navier-Stokes solver of the cylinder lesson (h=D/10, 12D×6D) runs for 60 time units, then tracks 200 coconuts released 0.6 to 1.4 D behind the cylinder centre for another 100 D/U, which is about 17 shedding periods at Re=100.

Case Wake Coconuts still within 4D behind after 100 D/U
Re=30 steady bubble, reversed flow up to 2.70 D behind the rear 200 of 200
Re=100 shedding (St≈0.17) 0 of 200
  1. At Re=30 the centreline cross-flow at the end is 3×10−5: steady, and every coconut stays.
  2. Deviation from the curriculum: the plan said Re=40. In this coarse model the smoothed mask acts as a slightly fatter body and the wake already sheds at 40 (at Re=40 only 125 of 200 coconuts stay for 40 time units), although a real cylinder stays steady up to about Re=47. So the trapping run uses Re=30.
  3. The bubble is longer than the unconfined value (about 1.5D at Re=30), again because of the coarse body and the 1/6 blockage.
  4. In the widget’s Föppl model, with ε=0, 80 of 80 coconuts stay for 200 a/U with the pair at 1.4a, 2a and 2.6a; with ε=0.3 and the pair at x0​=2a, 72 of 80 remain after 100 a/U, and with ε=0.6 none remain after 200.

Exercise 1How long is many cycles?

A 1 m boulder in a 0.5 m/s stream sheds with St=0.2. How long does a coconut that stays for 20 shedding cycles circle behind it?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. f=StU/D=0.2×0.5/1=0.1 Hz, a period of 10 s.
  2. 20 cycles is 200 s, over three minutes. (At Re=5×105 the real wake is turbulent, but the shedding frequency is still close to St≈0.2.)
